newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern heads to court an underdog.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern heads to court an underdog.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. will be the underdog when the merger battle for Conrail Inc. enters a federal courtroom Monday, but a loss there may be a temporary setback, takeover experts said.
"They (Norfolk Southern) have got an uphill struggle," said Charles Yablon, an expert on corporate law at Cardozo Law School in New York.

At the hearing starting on Monday in U.S. District Court, Norfolk Southern will seek to block CSX Corp.'s offer to buy 19.9 percent of Conrail stock from shareholders for $110 a share in the first step of a planned $8.5 billion cash-and-stock merger.
Norfolk Southern has made a rival all-cash offer of $110 a share valued at $10 billion.

A takeover stock specialist said Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern "could lose the battle, and win the war. If they win (in court), it's a super home run for them, and if they don't, it wasn't part of their strategy to begin with."

Norfolk Southern is seeking to snatch Philadelphia-based Conrail from Richmond, Va.-based CSX, Conrail's intended merger partner, in a battle over which company will become the dominant rail carrier in the huge market of the Northeast.

Norfolk Southern must pierce what CSX, according to Norfolk Southern, has described as a "bulletproof" merger pact protected by anti-takeover provisions and Pennsylvania corporate law that allows a company's board to consider factors other than shareholder interests in choosing a merger partner.

"I think it's going to be tough for Norfolk Southern to overcome the Pennsylvania state law," said Eric Orts, a corporate law professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School. "CSX and Conrail are going to argue (that) it's just not the court's job to second-guess the boards of directors."
The court hearing was expected to last all day Monday and possibly continue into Tuesday. Among several witnesses expected to testify is Conrail Chairman David LeVan.
Documents in the case have been sealed under court order, although Norfolk Southern has filed a motion seeking to lift the seal.
Norfolk Southern spokesman Robert Fort, while declining to discuss specifics, said the company's case would focus on arguments that shareholder interests must be honoured.
"We feel there has been an inappropriate, improper interpretation of the law ... so that shareholders are just not having an opportunity to exercise their rights," he said.

Conrail representatives declined to discuss the case. But Conrail has said in court papers that Norfolk Southern's challenge was legally defective and that the terms of the CSX deal were authorised under Pennsylvania law.

Norfolk Southern's main hope in court -- although it is a long shot -- may lie in the large difference between the two bids, analysts said. That could make it harder for Conrail to justify its preference for the CSX offer.

"If you have a significant difference between the two deals, and Conrail is bound and determined to go with the CSX deal ... you're bound to have angry shareholders," said Charles Vincent at PNC Institutional Investment Services.
"I suspect that's probably in the back of the mind of the judge who's got to rule on some of these motions," Vincent said, adding the judge might be inclined to let the shareholders decide the issue.

Norfolk Southern also has argued in court papers that allowing the CSX tender offer, which expires Wednesday, to proceed will trigger a chain of events that will make it impossible for Conrail shareholders to block the merger.

Conrail may argue, in addition to the discretion given under Pennsylvania law, that the only issue at stake is the bid for 19.9 percent of its shares, and that this does not threaten any "irreparable harm" to Norfolk Southern, which would be required to justify blocking the deal, analysts said.

If Conrail and CSX prevail in court, the deal must win approval from Conrail shareholders. They would be asked to waive a state law requiring a company to pay cash for all the shares of a takeover candidate once it has bought 20 percent.
A waiver would allow CSX to proceed with its plan to boost its Conrail stake to 40 percent stake buying shares for cash, then acquire the rest in a stock swap.

Shareholders may be reluctant to vote for the waiver -- with the prospect they could get all cash if Norfolk Southern were to prevail, analysts said. The Conrail-CSX pact prevents Conrail from accepting a rival bid before July 12, 1997.
"The shareholders are not going to vote for an opt-out," said the takeover stock trader.
